summary:
We built Earth Information Jukebox because scientific data about our planet is often presented in ways that feel distant and abstract. Numbers, charts, and graphs can show that the Earth is changing, but they rarely make us feel it. We wanted to change that.

Our challenge was simple but ambitious: how do you make climate data something people can truly experience? Our answer was sonification. Instead of only reading temperature values, we map them into sound. Temperature becomes pitch, change becomes rhythm, and value becomes volume. Using real NASA POWER observations from Jakarta, we turn daily measurements into an evolving sonic landscape that anyone can hear.

This project matters because climate change is one of the most important issues of our time, yet it is often communicated in ways that fail to engage people emotionally. By combining visualization, sound, and interactive design, Earth Information Jukebox offers another way to perceive patterns, changes, and relationships within Earth observations. We hope this approach can make scientific information more accessible, more memorable, and more human — especially for people who may not normally interact with large scientific datasets. This is not just a visualization. It is a way to listen to the Earth.
details:
https://github.com/Farel886/Astro-Gokil-Pisan

Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web experience that transforms NASA Earth observations into sound. Instead of reading temperature data as numbers on a screen, users can hear it. The project fetches real daily air temperature readings (T2M) from NASA POWER for Jakarta, Indonesia, and maps each value into musical properties: temperature becomes pitch, change between readings becomes rhythm and duration, and value becomes volume. The result is an evolving sonic landscape that reflects how our climate is changing over time.

The project works through a Next.js application with a server-side API route that calls the NASA POWER API. On the frontend, the Web Audio API generates real-time tones based on the data, while Canvas 2D draws a live waveform that reacts to playback. Users can explore the Earth Data dashboard, listen to the sonification engine, follow the sun across the globe in the Solar Time Lab (built with React Three Fiber and SunCalc), and travel through 46 years of warming in the Climate Time Machine. A built-in AI assistant called Farrel AI helps users understand the data and the project.

The main benefit is accessibility. Scientific data can feel abstract and distant, especially for people who do not normally interact with large datasets. By combining visualization and sonification, Earth Information Jukebox lets users experience the same information through more than one sense. This makes climate patterns more memorable, more emotional, and more human.

The intended impact is to change how people perceive Earth data. We want people to not only see that the planet is warming, but to feel it and hear it. This project is not about turning data into music for entertainment. It is about creating another way to perceive patterns, changes, and relationships within Earth observations.

We used Next.js, React, the Web Audio API, Canvas 2D, React Three Fiber, SunCalc, and the NASA POWER API. The project is deployed on Vercel and the source code is available on GitHub.

What makes this project creative is the idea itself: treating data as sound rather than only as visuals. Most climate visualizations stop at charts and graphs. We go further by giving data a voice. We also added interactive pages like the Solar Time Lab and the Climate Time Machine to let users explore Earth science from different angles.

Our team considered several factors: accuracy of the NASA data, clarity of the sonification mapping, accessibility across devices, and the emotional impact of the experience. We wanted the project to be scientifically grounded but also engaging for people who are not scientists. Every design decision, from the color palette to the sound mapping, was made with that balance in mind.
